what: IES Holdings is a group of electrical and mechanical contracting businesses. Its crews wire data centres, install electrical systems in new houses, build switchboards and custom power assemblies, and fit out commercial and industrial buildings.
customers: Data centre developers, homebuilders, industrial plant owners and commercial contractors, mostly across the southern and western United States.
money: Electrical infrastructure for data centres and high-tech industrial facilities.
Electrical installation in single-family and multi-family housing.
Custom power assemblies, switchgear, generator enclosures and commercial electrical work.
moat: Skilled electricians are the bottleneck in building data centres, and IES has the crews and the relationships with developers who need them now. The custom power assembly business makes equipment with long lead times, which gives it pricing power while demand exceeds capacity.
risks: Only one analyst covers the stock, and that single $440.00 target against a $166.90 price is not a consensus in any useful sense. It should be disregarded as evidence.
The residential segment depends on new housing starts, which are sensitive to mortgage rates.
Free cash flow of $228.4M is well below net income of $457.9M, as working capital grows with the order book.
Contracting is a fixed-price business: underestimating labour or materials on a large project turns a profit into a loss.
The data centre boom is the main growth driver, and a pause in hyperscaler spending would be felt quickly.
opportunities: Revenue has more than doubled, from $1.5B in 2021 to $3.4B in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $4.0B.
The shares trade at about 14.8 times earnings, low for a company growing this fast.
The balance sheet is almost debt-free: $88.1M of debt against $231.8M of cash, rare in contracting.
Electrician shortages mean capacity, not demand, is the limit, which supports margins.
watch: Backlog. In contracting, the order book tells you next year's revenue, and for IES it also shows how much of the data centre build-out it has actually won rather than merely bid on.
